summary: A survey of research on peer-to-peer networking, concentrating on search methods and placing them within a taxonomy. It stresses robustness as the key to using P2P beyond casual file sharing. It is an informational research overview.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4981 reviews the research on how peer-to-peer networks find data. It sorts the designs into three kinds of index, compares the network shapes used for exact lookups, reviews keyword search and richer queries, and asks how well each one keeps working when computers fail or leave.

questions: peer to peer search methods survey
subtitle: A survey of how peer-to-peer networks find data, and how well they survive failures.

tldr.problem: Peer-to-peer networks promise to aggregate huge amounts of storage and processing, but that only pays off outside casual file sharing if they stay reliable while nodes come and go.
tldr.mechanism: The survey sorts the literature into local, centralized and distributed indexes, then compares distributed hash tables, semantic indexes and richer queries, and asks how each design behaves under failure.
tldr.outcome: Its central finding is that robustness depends more on the low-level routines that maintain routes than on the shape of the network, and that the field has no agreed measures for reliability.

today: RFC 4981 is an Informational document and is not listed as obsoleted or updated. It was adapted from a paper in Elsevier's Computer Networks, volume 51, number 7, 2007, and it records the state of the research literature at that time.

sections.title: Introduction: What a Peer-to-Peer Network Is
sections.content:
A peer-to-peer (P2P) network has three characteristics. It self-organizes, which means it adapts automatically to the arrival, departure and failure of nodes. Communication is symmetric, because peers act as both clients and servers. And control is distributed, with no centralized directory or control point. USENET servers and BGP peers have these traits too, but the survey concentrates on the research wave since 2000, with Gnutella, Freenet, Pastry, Tapestry, Chord, the Content Addressable Network (CAN), pSearch and Edutella as leading examples.

The survey was written because the volume of work was large: one research database listed over 5,800 P2P publications. P2P can aggregate enormous storage and processing resources while keeping entry and scaling costs low, which is why it is described as potentially disruptive. The authors argue that the potential will not be realized in applications other than casual file sharing unless robustness is demonstrated, because failures are common across massive numbers of distributed peers.

The taxonomy in Figure 1 divides the literature along four lines: search, storage, security and applications. The survey covers search. A P2P search network consists of an underlying index, covered in sections 2 to 4, and the queries that propagate over that index, covered in section 5. Two questions run through the document: how do P2P search networks work, and how robust are they.
sections.plainLanguage: A peer-to-peer network has no central server. Its computers join and leave on their own, and each one both asks for and offers things. This survey asks how such networks find information, and how well they keep working when computers fail or walk away.

sections.title: Three Ways to Arrange the Index
sections.content:
The survey classifies a P2P index as local, centralized or distributed. With a local index a peer keeps references only to its own data, so queries have to travel widely; the early Gnutella design epitomized this. With a centralized index a single server keeps references to data on many peers, as Napster did. With a distributed index, pointers towards the target sit at several nodes, as in Freenet. Distributed indexes are used in most designs nowadays, so they dominate the survey.

A second cut separates non-forwarding indexes from forwarding ones. When queries are guided by a non-forwarding index they jump to the node holding the target data in a single hop; such schemes exist for both semantic and semantic-free indexes and have been extended to two hops where very large peer counts are needed. Forwarding indexes are the common case, where the number of hops varies with the number of peers, often logarithmically. The trade-offs between routing state, lookup latency, update bandwidth and peer churn are what decide how dependable the system is.

Measurement studies of the systems that used local indexes found that a very small percentage of peers had a very high degree, so the dependability of the whole system rested on those peers. The designers of Scamp turned that observation into a design heuristic, that the degree of each node should be nearly the same size. Analysing a system of N peers with mean degree c.log(n) and independent link failures of probability e, they showed that the probability of graph disconnection goes to zero as N grows if d is fixed and c is above (1+d)/(-log(e)), and to one if c is below (1-d)/(-log(e)).
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to arrange where the list of available data lives: only on the machine that owns it, on one central server, or spread across many machines. The spread-out arrangement is now the usual one, but measurement showed that a few heavily connected peers can carry the reliability of the whole network.

sections.title: Semantic-Free Indexes: Distributed Hash Tables
sections.content:
A distributed hash table (DHT) finds an object's persistent key in a very large, changing set of hosts without understanding what the key means. It is oblivious to whether a key names a document title, a piece of metadata or a line of text. The survey lists four design goals: low degree, so that each node keeps routing information for only a small number of other nodes and the impact of nodes arriving and departing is contained; low hop count; greedy routing, where each hop moves the query closer to the target; and robustness, so that a path to the target is found even when links or nodes fail.

Three contributions from the 1990s shaped later designs. Plaxton, Rajaraman and Richa gave a scheme that locates objects using fixed-length routing tables, with a 160-bit key as an example and every node acting as the root of a spanning tree, where a message routes towards an object by matching longer address suffixes. Its drawbacks are that global knowledge is needed to construct the overlay, an object's root node is a single point of failure, nodes cannot be inserted and deleted, and there is no mechanism to steer queries away from congestion hot spots. Consistent hashing, introduced for the Web caching problem, is smooth: when caches are added or deleted, the minimum number of object references move so as to maintain load balancing, and buckets may be added in any order. The Scalable Distributed Data Structure and its LH* algorithm satisfy three requirements: files grow to new servers only when existing servers are well loaded, there is no centralized directory, and the basic operations never require atomic updates to multiple clients.

Dependability is the survey's central concern, and the DHT literature yields four observations. First, static dependability comparisons show that no O(log n) DHT geometry is significantly more dependable than the other O(log n) geometries; ring, XOR and de Bruijn graphs all permit flexible choice of both neighbours and alternative routes, but only in de Bruijn are the alternate paths independent of each other. Second, dynamic dependability comparisons show that DHT dependability is sensitive to the underlying topology maintenance algorithms, which the survey groups by how nodes join and leave, how failures are first detected, how topology updates are shared, and how a node reacts when it receives one. Third, most DHTs assume nodes are ephemeral, with expected lifetimes of one to two hours, and therefore use an O(log n) geometry, while the O(1) hop designs suit stable nodes and deserve more research attention. Fourth, the study of DHT dependability is not yet a mature science, but recent simulation and formal development tools are helping it.
sections.plainLanguage: A distributed hash table stores keys without knowing what they mean, so a lookup finds any key that exists. It is built to keep each node's list of neighbours short, to reach the target in few steps, and to still find a way there when something breaks. The survey's summary is that the shape of the network matters less to reliability than the routine that keeps the routes up to date.

sections.title: Routing Geometries Compared
sections.content:
Six geometries carry most of the key-lookup designs. Plaxton trees are used by Pastry and Tapestry. Pastry keeps O(log n) neighbours and routes to a target in O(log n) hops, holding a leaf set of node identifiers on either side of its own and a routing table whose rows point to the node with a matching prefix. Tapestry remedies several weaknesses of the original Plaxton scheme: several root nodes per object instead of one, the ability to insert and delete nodes, incremental choice of root nodes through surrogate routing, and the ability to place object copies near peers that generate high query loads. Rings are used by Chord and Distributed K-ary Search (DKS). Chord maps nodes and keys onto an identifier ring, each peer tracking a predecessor, a list of successors and a finger table; every hop closes at least half the remaining distance around the ring, giving an average lookup hop count of (1/2)log n, and a periodic stabilization routine keeps the pointers current. Tori are used by CAN, which arranges a virtual d-dimensional Cartesian coordinate space on a d-torus, gives each node responsibility for a zone, and keeps the number of neighbours independent of system size, with O(d) neighbours and O(dn^(1/d)) hops.

Butterflies are used by Viceroy, which has constant degree like CAN and logarithmic diameter like Chord, and whose original paper explicitly assumed that peers do not fail. de Bruijn graphs are used by D2B, Koorde, Distance Halving and ODRI; a de Bruijn graph of degree k achieves an asymptotically optimal diameter of log n, and with O(log n) neighbours per node the hop count is O(log n/log log n). The survey illustrates the gap with a network of one million nodes of degree 20, where Chord has a diameter of 20 and de Bruijn a diameter of 5. Skip graphs augment skip lists with several ordered lists at each level, so that every node participates in one list at each level, which gives redundancy and supports prefix, proximity and range searches, at the cost of many more pointers per node than a DHT counterpart needs.
sections.plainLanguage: The survey compares six shapes for the network. They differ in how many neighbours each node keeps and how many steps a lookup takes. The de Bruijn shape reaches a target in the fewest steps, the tori shape keeps the fewest neighbours, and the skip graph shape is the only one that can search by name prefix or by range instead of by an exact key.

sections.title: Semantic Indexes: Keyword Search and Ranking
sections.content:
A semantic index captures the relationships between object names, content and metadata, which a DHT does not do. It makes rich queries possible, but because its design is often driven by heuristics it may not guarantee that scarce items are found. The survey frames the opportunity as graduated data independence, consistency and query flexibility, with probabilistically complete query responses, across very large numbers of low-cost, geographically distributed, dynamic nodes.

Keyword lookup is classified by three things: how the query is routed, through flooding, policy-based choice of the next hop, or random walks; how it is forwarded, through iterative unicast searches of ultrapeers or recursively; and how the flow is controlled, through tokens granted by receivers, throttling by the sender when receivers discard packets, or a dynamic time-to-live that the sender adjusts from the number of results received, the number of connections left and the number of nodes already theoretically reached. The index itself may be partitioned by document, by keyword using an inverted list, or by both. The main Gnutella improvement was the Query Routing Table, a forwarded index of filename keywords that lets ultrapeers send a leaf only the queries it can match, and which is compressed by hashing under the Query Routing Protocol.

One system, Gia, combined receiver-based flow control, a biased random walk and one-hop replication, and reported a 2-4 orders of magnitude improvement in query success rates in churning networks. The robustness metrics it used were the collapse point, the per-node query rate at which the successful query rate falls below 90%, and the average hop count immediately before collapse. Information retrieval work adds ranking: the vector model represents documents and queries as term vectors weighted by term frequency, inverse document frequency and document length, and PlanetP, FASD, pSearch and eSearch apply it in peer-to-peer settings. Latent semantic indexing, used by pSearch, maps both vectors into a concept space with fewer dimensions using singular value decomposition, but its retrieval quality is inherently inferior to Okapi weighting for large collections and the decomposition consumes excessive memory and computation time, so the later pSearch work searches with Okapi while keeping latent semantic indexing to group similar documents near each other. The survey notes that a search of the proceedings of the annual ACM conference on information retrieval for the words reliable, available, dependable or adaptable returned no results at the time of writing.
sections.plainLanguage: A semantic index understands words, so a user can ask for several keywords at once instead of an exact key. Such indexes answer richer questions, but they are built on heuristics, so they may miss rare results. Ranking methods borrowed from library science decide which answer comes first, and the survey notes that almost none of that work has been tested for reliability.

sections.title: Richer Queries and Recommendations for Research
sections.content:
Distributed hash tables mostly support exact-match, single-key queries. Skip graphs support range and prefix queries but not aggregation. The survey reviews early work on range queries, which need the key space to stay ordered, so randomized hashing works against them; on multi-attribute queries, where one answer must satisfy several conditions; on join queries, which combine records from two collections; and on aggregation queries such as count, sum, maximum, minimum, average, median and top-k, which combine results across a tree of nodes. The design choices for aggregation trees are how the overlay uses DHTs, how the tree repairs itself when there are failures, how many aggregation trees there are, and whether the tree is static or dynamic.

The security considerations section is short: the document addresses P2P search, points to its own taxonomy for references on P2P security, and recommends storage, security and applications for further investigation.

The survey closes with four suggestions. The companion surveys for storage, security and applications should be completed. P2P indexes are maturing while P2P queries are still embryonic, with work on more expressive queries starting to gain momentum in 2003 but remaining fraught with efficiency and load issues. The low-level mechanisms that affect robustness should be isolated, because comparing the robustness of geometries such as rings against de Bruijn graphs has limited value when robustness is so sensitive to the topology maintenance algorithms underneath. And the field should build consensus on robustness metrics and their acceptable ranges, from the median query path length for a failure of a given percentage of nodes, through bisection width, path overlap, lookup latency, successful routing rates and lookup failure rates, to clustering measures such as edge expansion and node expansion.
sections.plainLanguage: Most peer-to-peer indexes answer one exact key and nothing else. The survey reviews the first work on asking for ranges, several conditions at once, or totals across the network, and finds the field still embryonic. It ends with four asks for researchers: survey the rest of the field, study the harder query types, test the low-level routines that decide robustness, and agree on how robustness should be measured.
